assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Time period, T
items.clue: How long one complete revolution takes.

items.label: Elastic collision
items.clue: Total kinetic energy is the same before and after.

items.label: Conservation of linear momentum
items.clue: The total for a system stays constant unless a resultant external force acts.

items.label: Centripetal force
items.clue: The resultant, pointing inward along the radius, that is needed for circular motion.

questions.stem: An ice-hockey puck is struck and then slides across horizontal ice. Friction and air resistance on the puck are negligible. What happens to the motion of the puck after it has left the stick?

options.text: It slows gradually as the force from the stick is used up.
It continues in a straight line at a constant speed.
It slows and stops, as moving bodies come to rest naturally.
It stops at once, since nothing now pushes it along its path.

questions.explanation: Newton's first law: with no resultant force, the velocity of the puck is constant, so it moves in a straight line at constant speed. The stick exerted a force only while in contact; no force is needed to keep the puck moving.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown vertically upwards. Air resistance is negligible. Which force or forces act on the ball while it is still rising, after it has left the hand?

options.text: Its weight and a decreasing upward force from the throw
Its weight and an upward force larger than its weight
No force until it stops at the top and then starts to fall
Only its weight, the downward pull of the Earth

questions.explanation: Once the ball leaves the hand, the only body still interacting with it is the Earth (air resistance is negligible). Its weight acts downwards throughout the flight, which is why the ball slows as it rises.

questions.stem: A box is pulled at constant velocity across a rough horizontal floor by a rope that makes an angle of 30° above the horizontal. Which list gives all the forces that should appear on a free-body diagram of the box, and no others?

options.text: Weight, normal force, tension, friction, push of box on floor
Weight, normal force, tension, friction, forward force of motion
Weight, normal force, rope tension and friction from the floor
Weight, tension and friction; the rigid floor exerts no push up

questions.explanation: A free-body diagram shows every force that other bodies exert ON the box: the Earth (weight F_g), the floor (normal force F_N and friction F_f) and the rope (tension T). Nothing else touches the box or exerts a field force on it.

questions.stem: A book rests on a horizontal table. The weight of the book is the gravitational force exerted on it by the Earth. Which force forms a Newton's third law pair with this weight?

options.text: The normal force exerted on the book by the table
The contact force exerted on the table by the book
The gravitational force exerted on the Earth by the book
No force, because the book is too small to pull the Earth

questions.explanation: A third-law pair is the two forces of ONE interaction, here the gravitational interaction between the book and the Earth. The Earth pulls the book down; the book pulls the Earth up with a force of equal magnitude. The two forces are of the same type and act on different bodies.

questions.stem: A car of mass 1.2 × 10³ kg travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ collides head-on with a truck of mass 1.2 × 10⁴ kg travelling at 10 m s⁻¹. How does the force exerted by the truck on the car compare with the force exerted by the car on the truck during the collision?

options.text: The truck's force is larger, since the truck has more mass.
They are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
The car's force is larger, since the car is moving faster.
The truck's force is larger, since the car's velocity changes more.

questions.explanation: The two forces are the two sides of one interaction between the car and the truck, so by Newton's third law they are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, whatever the masses and speeds.

questions.stem: A person stands on the floor of a lift that is accelerating upwards. Which description of a correct free-body diagram for the person is right?

options.text: Two arrows: the weight downwards and a normal force of equal size from the floor upwards.
Two arrows: the weight downwards and a larger normal force from the floor upwards.
Three arrows: the weight, the normal force, and an upward force of the lift's motion.
Three arrows: the weight, the normal force, and the person's push down on the floor.

questions.stem: A lamp of mass 5.0 kg hangs at rest, supported by two cables, one on each side. Each cable makes an angle of 40° with the horizontal, and the arrangement is symmetrical. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the tension in each cable?
questions.explanation: The lamp is in translational equilibrium, so the resultant force is zero. The horizontal components of the tensions cancel. Vertically, 2T sin 40° = mg, so T = (5.0 × 9.8 N)/(2 × 0.643) = 38 N.
